overview: Brushed Pottery culture is a modern archaeological label, not a recovered self-name, kingdom, tribe, language, or border. Researchers use it for changing patterns in handmade ceramics, settlements, buildings, tools, food remains, and craft evidence across parts of the eastern Baltic. The atlas shows one identical polygon from 500 BCE to 200 CE. Scholarship usually begins the longer tradition centuries earlier and often carries its late phase into the third century CE, so both atlas endpoints are software choices. The inherited summary compresses this into one Bronze Age culture succeeding Narva and speculates about what made every brush mark; those claims need qualification. Excavations reveal fortified hilltops, open settlements, post-built houses, hearths, crops, livestock, fishing, bone and antler work, bronze casting, iron use, and wide exchange. They reveal much less about kinship, childhood, healing, personal identity, toilets, or spoken language. No securely attributable sentence, inscription, script, or named word survives from people assigned this label. The map layer therefore organizes evidence for teaching without turning pottery into a passport or its polygon into a state.

periods.title: 500 to 400 BCE: the atlas enters an older tradition
periods.summary: The exact feature first appears at 500 BCE, although eastern Baltic brushed or striated pottery and fortified settlements began much earlier. Its fixed polygon is a teaching layer, not a founding frontier. Households used livestock, crops, fishing, hunting, stone, bone, antler, bronze, and handmade vessels in locally varied combinations.

periods.title: 400 to 300 BCE: hillfort life was not one blueprint
periods.summary: Fortified sites combined slopes, fences, ditches, buildings, hearths, storage, and work areas differently. Open sites also mattered. Identical atlas geometry through 400, 323, and 300 BCE cannot show local rebuilding, abandonment, seasonal movement, or uneven excavation. Archaeologists reconstruct those changes from contexts rather than map seams.

periods.title: 300 to 200 BCE: later pottery and iron gain visibility
periods.summary: Late brushed pottery styles are often dated from the third century BCE, while iron tools and changing ceramic forms become more visible. This was not an instant technological switch. Stone, bone, antler, bronze, and iron could coexist, and old objects or mixed layers complicate any neat progress chart.

periods.title: 200 to 100 BCE: settlement networks diversify
periods.summary: Surveys along the Neris and excavations elsewhere reveal hillforts, foot settlements, lakeshores, and unenclosed sites with different functions and durations. Communities did not all move together. A pot style may connect practices across places, but it cannot prove one administration, ruler, kin group, or synchronized migration.

periods.title: 100 to 1 BCE: makers sustain and alter traditions
periods.summary: Potters selected clay, temper, vessel form, surface treatment, and firing practice; metalworkers managed heat, moulds, crucibles, and reusable metal. Such skills required observation and teaching. Similar products can reflect communication or shared habits, while microscopic differences warn against imagining one centralized workshop for the entire polygon.

periods.title: 1 BCE to 100 CE: new settlement patterns emerge
periods.summary: During the early centuries CE, foot and open settlements became more prominent beside older hillfort traditions. Roman-period objects and neighboring ceramic styles entered local contexts selectively. Exchange widened choices without converting inhabitants into Romans or making imported goods a census of wealth, language, ethnicity, or political loyalty.

periods.title: 100 to 150 CE: farming and craft leave sharper traces
periods.summary: Late settlements preserve postholes, fences, charred crops, animal bones, pottery, daub, crucibles, and metalworking debris. At Skudeniai, dated occupation overlaps and extends beyond this window. These finds illuminate activities, yet preservation and excavation sample only fragments of meals, work, social ties, illness, and belief.

periods.title: 150 to 200 CE: transformation outlasts the polygon
periods.summary: Narkunai was abandoned around the late second century, while other late settlements continued and brushed pottery remained in use into the third century in some schemes. At 200 CE the atlas removes the label. Fire layers, migration, internal change, and cultural interaction remain site-specific explanations, not one documented ending event.

items.text: The exact indexed id is brushed-pottery-culture, dated approximately 500 BCE to 200 CE and already typed as culture. Coverage finds eight exact feature intervals and no finished card. These are atlas metadata, not the date when a people began, named themselves, drew borders, or disappeared.

An archaeological culture groups recurring material patterns across a region and period. It is an analytical tool made by researchers. Similar pots, buildings, or tools may track learned practices and contact, but they do not automatically reveal one ethnic group, language, ancestry, government, or shared name.

All eight target snapshots decode to the same single Polygon: one ring, 39 positions, and a bounding box from about 21.86 to 29.89 east and 51.98 to 57.76 north. Thirteen probes fall inside. Repetition shows reused atlas artwork, not seven centuries of surveyed border stability.

The inherited summary calls the culture simply Bronze Age and says it succeeded Narva. Lithuanian scholarship instead describes a long late Bronze, early Iron, and early Roman-period sequence with multiple contributing traditions and regional phases. The card keeps the exact map interval while correcting that compressed history.

Later writers often connect the material to Baltic histories, but a pottery category cannot supply an individual's self-identification or spoken language. The card therefore uses people, communities, households, and makers assigned to this archaeological label. It does not back-project modern Lithuanian, Latvian, or Belarusian nationality.

Hillfort is convenient shorthand, yet sites varied in position, enclosure, occupation length, and function. Some held buildings and repeated work; some may have offered refuge; some were reoccupied after gaps. A rampart is evidence of construction and concern, not proof of a king, army, capital, or permanent town.

Neris valley surveys compare hillforts, open settlements, environmental settings, size, chronology, and later burial grounds. The resulting network is more informative than one famous hilltop. Survey visibility and modern land use still bias what is found, so blank spaces on a map need not have been empty.

Skudeniai was a briefly occupied unenclosed settlement on a moraine rise, with activity extending toward a wet hollow or former small lake. Postholes and fences organized space without a defensive crown. This exact site is late, showing that brushed pottery did not require every household to live inside a hillfort.

Lake Luokesas preserves wooden piles and organic traces because waterlogged conditions differ from dry hilltops. Its settlements date roughly 800 to 400 BCE, mostly before this card, and cannot represent every Brushed Pottery community. They provide deep regional comparison for building skill, wetland travel, and preservation bias.

Kernave is a long-lived cultural landscape with occupations far earlier and later than this card. Brushed Pottery layers are one part of that sequence. Later castles and medieval importance cannot be projected backward, while early sherds and structures should not be treated as miniature versions of the later town.

The label comes from visible striations on handmade vessel surfaces. Potters also varied wall thickness, rim shape, paste, temper, smoothing, polishing, and firing. Archaeologists debate tools and purposes behind surface traces; the inherited suggestion that bundles of grass or straw made every mark is not secure enough to universalize.

Skudeniai pottery includes coarse striated wares, finer polished vessels, and other surface treatments made with related clay-preparation traditions. Petrography studies inclusions invisible to casual inspection. A surface name therefore captures only one feature of a much richer technical sequence from raw clay to use, breakage, and deposition.

At Narkunai, researchers classified 14,879 sherds and examined spatial relationships among pottery, postholes, hearths, bones, and metalworking remains. Sherd concentrations may trace activities or abandonment, but layers were formed by people, fire, trampling, repair, dumping, later occupation, excavation, and preservation together.

Macroscopic and microscopic pottery analysis can identify forming choices, mineral inclusions, firing conditions, use, and repair more reliably than style alone. Those choices may be learned within communities and shared across them. They still cannot name a potter, assign a mother tongue, or prove that all similar vessels had identical contents.

A cooking pot might be brushed, polished, soot-darkened, patched, or broken; none of those traits makes it a prehistoric identity card. The gentle joke carries a serious rule: classification helps compare evidence, while people could borrow techniques, move, marry, exchange vessels, or make something unusual without changing citizenship.

sections.title: Homes, hearths, fences, and shared work

items.text: Narkunai's lower layer contained scattered rectangular post-built structures with round stone hearths. A woven barrier between two rows of posts was strengthened with stone paving. These remains show planning, timber work, fuel use, and coordinated maintenance, though one excavated plan cannot establish a standard household size.

Postholes at Skudeniai indicate buildings and fences, but archaeologists identify plans by pattern, depth, alignment, and associated finds rather than by one hole. Repairs and repeated occupation can overlap. Reconstructing walls and roofs therefore involves tested inference, not simply connecting every surviving dot into the tidiest possible house.

At Reskutenai, fourth-to-fifth-century remains include semi-subterranean irregular rectangular buildings, clay-coated walls, an outdoor stone hearth, weights, a spindle whorl, pottery, and an iron knife. Because this occupation is later than the atlas endpoint, it informs regional transformation rather than serving as a direct 500 BCE household plan.

Soil chemistry at a disturbed southeastern Lithuanian hilltop detected human-related signals even in some features lacking artefacts, yet no single function could be assigned confidently. Phosphorus, metals, magnetic susceptibility, soil movement, and later disturbance can sharpen interpretation while also warning against naming every stain a hearth, store, or home.

Building posts, gathering timber, renewing fences, tending hearths, moving stores, and repairing roofs required many hands. Archaeology can demonstrate labor and coordination more securely than who commanded it. A defended enclosure might express risk, cooperation, status, storage needs, or several motives at once, rather than one centralized authority.

sections.title: Food, farming, animals, and seasonal choices

items.text: At late Skudeniai, charred plant remains included barley, wheat, millet, rye, and peas, with barley most abundant in the sampled assemblage. These are preserved crops, not a complete menu or field census. Charring, sampling, storage accidents, cleaning, and refuse movement strongly shape what survives.

Skudeniai's small animal-bone sample included cattle, sheep or goats, and pigs. Sparse bones support husbandry but not herd percentages for the entire culture. Butchery, marrow extraction, dogs, soil chemistry, disposal, recovery mesh, and preservation can all change the archaeological count before analysts ever identify a fragment.

At Late Bronze Age fortified sites in northeastern Lithuania, animal bones show livestock alongside fishing, mussel collecting, hunting, fur use, and bone working. These sites mostly predate the card but illuminate regional roots. Strategies differed between settlements, so no single recipe describes every century or household.

Stone axes, querns, sickles, animal remains, grains, and pollen can support farming interpretations, while each line has dating and recovery limits. Inland communities balanced cultivation, herding, fishing, gathering, hunting, and exchange differently. Environmental setting mattered, and production changed over the long life of the archaeological tradition.

Food work included planting, tending, harvesting, herding, fishing, gathering, slaughter, grinding, cooking, storing, serving, and cleaning. Finds reveal parts of that chain but rarely who performed each task. The card does not assign farming to men, pottery to women, or fishing to children without direct evidence.

sections.title: Families, social life, children, and learning

items.text: Buildings and activity areas show people living and working together, but a post pattern cannot reveal whether occupants were a nuclear family, extended kin, guests, apprentices, dependants, or another group. Household is used as an activity scale, not as proof of one marriage rule, inheritance system, residence pattern, or family size.

Pottery forming, firing, animal care, crop work, woodworking, fishing, weaving, bone shaping, and metal casting required practiced sequences. Skills were learned somehow through observation, participation, correction, memory, and repetition. Archaeology supports transmitted knowledge, but it does not preserve a school timetable, lesson plan, teacher title, or standard childhood stage.

Bone and antler artefacts from Narkunai, Nevieriske, and Kereliai preserve raw-material selection, unfinished pieces, waste, and manufacturing choices. Some copied metal forms, showing makers adapting prestigious designs in another material. This can suggest networks and social distinction, but not the age, gender, freedom, or ethnicity of each maker.

Settlement and burial objects can illuminate dress, ornaments, production, and exchange, yet Brushed Pottery burial customs remain poorly known. A mould or ornament at a dwelling site does not identify an elite woman, community leader, refugee, or craft specialist by itself. Such possibilities belong as questions, not reconstructed biographies.

Children almost certainly watched adults, practiced tasks, played, and carried responsibilities, but exact-period evidence does not securely identify a toy, classroom, initiation age, or child's personal voice for this label. The card includes learning while refusing invented chores. Even a very small pot is not automatically someone's homework.

sections.title: Health, illness, care, and evidence limits

items.text: Food diversity, shelter, fire, clothing, clean water access, cooperation, and stored supplies plausibly supported health. This is an inference from living conditions, not a diagnosis. Crop and animal remains cannot show that everyone ate equally, avoided hunger, absorbed nutrients similarly, or experienced the same seasonal risks.

Open hearths provided heat, light, cooking, and craft temperatures while producing smoke, sparks, burns, and indoor air risks. Hearth placement and house maintenance mattered, but archaeology rarely records ventilation behavior or exposure for one person. Fire layers can mark accidents, attack, clearing, or later disturbance rather than one certain disaster.

Human bones can preserve evidence of injury, disease, diet, workload, age, and care, but Brushed Pottery burial evidence is exceptionally sparse and disputed. Without a well-contextualized skeletal sample, population-wide health claims would be misleading. The absence of diagnosed disease in this card is absence of evidence, not perfect health.

Animal bone, horn, clay, stone, wood, fibre, and metal tools could support food preparation, clothing, shelter, mobility, and caregiving. A tool's possible medical use needs direct context, residue, wear, or comparison. The card does not turn an awl, knife, pin, or plant remain into a surgical instrument or remedy.

No reviewed source securely documents a named healer, medicine, dosage, childbirth practice, disability role, or specific treatment for communities assigned this label between 500 BCE and 200 CE. People certainly faced illness and cared for one another, but responsible history separates that human certainty from details the archaeological record cannot supply.

Sites occur near rivers, lakes, wetlands, and travel corridors, yet Skudeniai also stood away from a large water body while activity reached a wet hollow below. Communities needed drinking and cooking water, but the reviewed evidence does not establish one well design, purification method, storage rule, or daily allowance.

Waterlogged sites can preserve wooden piles, plant matter, leather, and other organic materials lost on dry hilltops. That exceptional survival can transform interpretation, but it also makes direct comparison uneven. Missing baskets, floors, containers, textiles, or food at another site may reflect decay rather than their historical absence.

Pits, dark layers, charcoal, broken pottery, animal bone, burnt stone, daub, and plant remains may record storage, cooking, craft, demolition, maintenance, or refuse. Context matters. At Skudeniai, some plant distributions did not fit refuse disposal, showing why archaeologists should not label every outside pit a rubbish bin.

Hearth ash, broken vessels, food scraps, manure, craft waste, and damaged building material required practical handling. Reuse, burning, sweeping, scattering, dumping, decay, and later ploughing leave different traces. Evidence for managed space is stronger than any claim for a universal cleanliness rule or organized municipal collection.

No reviewed excavation securely identifies a Brushed Pottery toilet, latrine design, sewer, drain network, or fecal-waste routine. Organic facilities may vanish, and excavated areas are incomplete. Limited evidence does not mean people lacked privacy or hygiene knowledge; it means the card should not draw a bathroom from a posthole.

Narkunai yielded crucibles, moulds, ladles, and household ceramics examined with imaging and chemical methods. Some pieces carried secure metal traces while miniature cups did not. That distinction matters: resemblance alone cannot prove a workshop tool. Metalworking knowledge joined local practice, mobile expertise, imported forms, and recyclable material.

Bronze casting in the southeastern Baltic used moulds for objects with wider regional parallels despite scarce local ore. Makers could reproduce foreign-looking forms locally, complicating simple imported-versus-native categories. Exchange moved raw material, finished objects, designs, and technical knowledge, while archaeology rarely identifies the exact route or status of a craftsperson.

Iron tools became more common during the late phases, but adoption was uneven and did not instantly replace stone, bone, antler, or bronze. Different materials served different tasks and values. A community using an iron knife and a stone implement was not stuck between ages; it was selecting from a practical toolkit.

Spindle whorls, weights, pins, ornaments, and fine pottery hint at fibre work, dress, display, and exchange. Their survival is selective, and some functions remain debated. Clothing itself usually decays. Researchers can discuss textile production and adornment without assigning every object to one gender, rank, ceremony, or permanent social class.

Achievements include durable building, landscape knowledge, farming, animal management, fishing, ceramic skill, organic-material craft, bronze casting, ironworking, exchange, and repeated adaptation. These are cumulative community accomplishments rather than discoveries by one named inventor. The evidence supports ingenuity without inventing rulers, heroic firsts, or a technological race against neighbors.

Written-language sample: none reproduced. No reviewed source provides a securely attributable sentence, inscription, script, or named word created by people assigned to this archaeological label between 500 BCE and 200 CE. Pottery striations are surface treatment, not translatable prose, and later Baltic languages are not projected backward.

The culture name was coined by archaeologists from material evidence; it was not recorded by an inhabitant. Classical authors' names for northern peoples would be outside labels and cannot automatically be matched to this polygon. Without a bilingual inscription, secure context, and defensible attribution, an attractive ancient word would mislead rather than teach.

At Kernave, fire and destruction layers accompany late change, while other sites show different dates and pathways. Researchers debate internal development, interaction, migration, and new material traditions. One burned hillfort cannot prove that the entire archaeological culture ended in a single invasion, battle, evacuation, epidemic, or ethnic replacement.

Reanalysis at Juodoniai overturned an overly smooth continuity story by examining stratigraphy, planigraphy, activity zones, and occupation gaps. New dates, microscopic pottery study, soil chemistry, botanical remains, and animal bones keep refining the picture. Archaeological labels are working models that should change when evidence improves.

People continued living across eastern Lithuania, Latvia, Belarus, and neighboring regions after 200 CE, but the atlas label disappears and material classifications change. Later communities and modern nations have their own histories. The responsible ending is transformation: practices, populations, and networks changed without a documented moment when everyone vanished or changed identity together.

ending.text: At 200 CE the exact brushed-pottery-culture polygon disappears from the atlas, while archaeological studies often carry late striated ware into the third century and sometimes later at particular sites. Narkunai, Kernave, Juodoniai, Skudeniai, and other settlements changed on different schedules. New pottery, ironworking, unenclosed settlements, foot settlements, burial traditions, exchange networks, movement, and local rebuilding altered how researchers classify the evidence. No source records one state falling or one named people becoming extinct. The endpoint is a map seam inside a longer regional transformation, so the card has no invented conqueror, predecessor, successor, or ethnic replacement arrow.
